title: Τοῦ συβώτου λόγος
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Eumaeus answers Odysseus's question about his parents. Laertes is still alive but prays to die, grieving for the son who is gone and for his wife, who has died of grief; Eumaeus recalls how she reared him beside her daughter Ctimene, and says that from the lady of the house, with the overweening men in it, he now hears nothing kind. Odysseus, still unrecognised, asks how Eumaeus came to be so far from home. Eumaeus bids him sit, drink and pass the long night trading sorrows, and begins his story: the island of Syrie, where his father Ctesius was king, the Phoenician traders who came there with trinkets, and the Phoenician woman of his father's house, whom one of them seduced. She tells the sailors where she is from and asks to be taken home, makes them swear to secrecy, and offers them gold and a child of the house to sell.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε συβώτης, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe sybōtēs, orchamos andrōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the swineherd, chief of men:
sentences.i: Then the swineherd, chief of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Eumaeus now answers Odysseus's question about his parents (15.347–350). τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the reply formula 'Him then in turn addressed': τόν is the pronoun 'him' (in Homer what later Greek calls the article is a pronoun), αὖτε 'in turn, again', προσέειπε the aorist of προσεῖπον 'address'. συβώτης 'swineherd' is built on σῦς 'pig'. ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν 'chief of men' is a leader's title, kept in the translation though it sits oddly on a swineherd.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, ξεῖνε, μάλ’ ἀτρεκέως ἀγορεύσω.
sentences.tr: toigar egō toi, xeine, mal’ atrekeōs agoreusō.
sentences.l: “Well then, I will tell you, stranger, very exactly.
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you, stranger, quite exactly.
sentences.n: This is Eumaeus's answer about Laertes and the household. τοιγάρ 'well then, accordingly' opens it. ἐγώ τοι is 'I ... to you', τοι being the epic enclitic form of σοι. ξεῖνε 'stranger' is the vocative. ἀτρεκέως 'exactly, without deviation' is the adverb of ἀτρεκής. ἀγορεύσω 'I will tell' can be read as a future or as a short-vowel aorist subjunctive.

sentences.t:
Λαέρτης μὲν ἔτι ζώει, Διὶ δ’ εὔχεται αἰεὶ
θυμὸν ἀπὸ μελέων φθίσθαι οἷς ἐν μεγάροισιν·
sentences.tr:
Laertēs men eti zōei, Dii d’ euchetai aiei
thymon apo meleōn phthisthai hois en megaroisin·
sentences.l:
Laertes, indeed, still lives, and to Zeus he prays always
that his life from his limbs may perish in his own halls;
sentences.i: Laertes is still alive, but he prays to Zeus always that his life may perish out of his limbs in his own halls;
sentences.n: Laertes is Odysseus's father; Eumaeus gives news of him first. ζώει is the uncontracted form of ζώω 'live' (Attic ζῇ). Διί is the dative of Ζεύς. εὔχεται 'prays' takes an infinitive that states the prayer: θυμὸν ἀπὸ μελέων φθίσθαι 'that his life perish from his limbs', φθίσθαι being the aorist middle infinitive of φθίνω 'perish, waste away'. θυμός here is the life that leaves the body, not the 'heart'. οἷς is the possessive ὅς, 'his own', agreeing with μεγάροισιν: a dative in -οισιν (Attic -οις), 'in his own halls'. αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί.

sentences.t:
ἐκπάγλως γὰρ παιδὸς ὀδύρεται οἰχομένοιο
κουριδίης τ’ ἀλόχοιο δαΐφρονος, ἥ ἑ μάλιστα
ἤκαχ’ ἀποφθιμένη καὶ ἐν ὠμῷ γήραϊ θῆκεν.
sentences.tr:
ekpaglōs gar paidos odyretai oichomenoio
kouridiēs t’ alochoio daïphronos, hē he malista
ēkach’ apophthimenē kai en ōmōi gēraï thēken.
sentences.l:
For terribly he laments for his son, who is gone,
and for his wedded wife, wise-minded, who most of all
grieved him by dying, and set him in raw old age.
sentences.i: For he laments terribly for his son, who is gone, and for his wedded wife, wise-hearted as she was, who by dying grieved him most of all and put him into a raw old age.
sentences.n: Both of Laertes's griefs are named: the son and the wife. ἐκπάγλως 'terribly' is the adverb of ἔκπαγλος 'dreadful'. ὀδύρεται 'laments' takes a genitive for what is mourned: παιδὸς οἰχομένοιο 'for a son who is gone' (οἴχομαι 'be gone'), and κουριδίης ἀλόχοιο δαΐφρονος 'for his wedded wife', ἀλόχοιο being a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου). δαΐφρων is 'wise-minded' if it comes from δαῆναι 'to know' and 'warlike' if from δάϊος 'hostile'; the meaning is disputed and the translation follows the first. ἥ ἑ μάλιστα ἤκαχ’ ἀποφθιμένη: ἥ 'who', ἑ 'him', ἤκαχε the aorist of ἀκαχίζω 'grieve', ἀποφθιμένη the aorist middle participle of ἀποφθίνω 'die'. ἐν ὠμῷ γήραϊ θῆκεν 'set him in raw old age': ὠμός 'raw' is here either 'cruel' or 'unripe, before its time', and the Greek does not choose.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἄχεϊ οὗ παιδὸς ἀπέφθιτο κυδαλίμοιο,
λευγαλέῳ θανάτῳ, ὡς μὴ θάνοι ὅς τις ἐμοί γε
ἐνθάδε ναιετάων φίλος εἴη καὶ φίλα ἔρδοι.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ acheï hou paidos apephthito kydalimoio,
leugaleōi thanatōi, hōs mē thanoi hos tis emoi ge
enthade naietaōn philos eiē kai phila erdoi.
sentences.l:
And she from grief for her own son, glorious, perished,
by a pitiful death — so may not die whoever, to me at least,
here dwelling, is dear, and does dear things.
sentences.i: And she died of grief for her own glorious son, by a pitiful death: may no one die so who lives here and is dear to me and does kindly things.
sentences.n: Eumaeus turns from Laertes's grief to the wife's death and then to a wish. ἡ δ’ is 'and she' (the pronoun). ἄχεϊ is the dative of ἄχος 'grief', and οὗ is the possessive 'her own' (ὅς, not the relative), genitive, agreeing with παιδός; κυδαλίμοιο is a genitive in -οιο from κυδάλιμος 'glorious'. ἀπέφθιτο is the aorist middle of ἀποφθίνω 'perish'. λευγαλέῳ θανάτῳ 'by a pitiful death' is a dative of means. ὡς μὴ θάνοι is a wish, with the optative: 'so may no one die'; ὅς τις 'whoever', ναιετάων 'dwelling' the uncontracted participle of ναιετάω, φίλα ἔρδοι 'may do kindly things' (ἔρδω 'do').

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὲν οὖν δὴ κείνη ἔην, ἀχέουσά περ ἔμπης,
τόφρα τί μοι φίλον ἔσκε μεταλλῆσαι καὶ ἐρέσθαι,
οὕνεκά μ’ αὐτὴ θρέψεν ἅμα Κτιμένῃ τανυπέπλῳ,
θυγατέρ’ ἰφθίμῃ, τὴν ὁπλοτάτην τέκε παίδων·
sentences.tr:
ophra men oun dē keinē eēn, acheousa per empēs,
tophra ti moi philon eske metallēsai kai eresthai,
houneka m’ autē threpsen hama Ktimenēi tanypeplōi,
thygater’ iphthimēi, tēn hoplotatēn teke paidōn·
sentences.l:
As long, then, as she was alive, grieving though she was, all the same,
so long somewhat dear to me it was to ask and to inquire,
because she herself reared me together with long-robed Ctimene,
her daughter, mighty, whom the youngest of her children she bore;
sentences.i: As long as she was alive, though grieving all the same, it pleased me to ask and inquire, because she herself brought me up together with long-robed Ctimene, her mighty daughter, whom she bore as the youngest of her children;
sentences.n: The 'she' of this unit is Odysseus's mother, whose death Eumaeus has just told. ὄφρα ... τόφρα 'as long as ... so long'. ἔην is ἦν 'was', κείνη is ἐκείνη; ἀχέουσά περ ἔμπης 'grieving though she was, all the same' (ἀχέω 'grieve'). ἔσκε is the iterative imperfect of εἰμί; τί is weak, 'somewhat'. μεταλλῆσαι and ἐρέσθαι are aorist infinitives, of μεταλλάω 'inquire' and ἔρομαι 'ask'. οὕνεκα is 'because'; μ’ is με; θρέψεν is ἔθρεψε(ν) without the augment, 'reared'. Κτιμένῃ τανυπέπλῳ is a dative: 'long-robed Ctimene'. θυγατέρ’ is best read as the dative θυγατέρι with its ι elided, agreeing with Κτιμένῃ and ἰφθίμῃ ('mighty'). Line 364 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρ’, short by nature, is lengthened to fill the long place of the first foot. τὴν ὁπλοτάτην τέκε παίδων: τήν is 'whom', ὁπλοτάτην 'youngest', τέκε the unaugmented aorist of τίκτω 'bore', παίδων 'of the children'.

sentences.t: τῇ ὁμοῦ ἐτρεφόμην, ὀλίγον δέ τί μ’ ἧσσον ἐτίμα.
sentences.tr: tēi homou etrephomēn, oligon de ti m’ hēsson etima.
sentences.l: With her together I was being reared, and a little less she honoured me.
sentences.i: I was brought up along with her, and she valued me only a little less.
sentences.n: τῇ is the pronoun 'her', in the dative, and ὁμοῦ 'together' goes with it. ἐτρεφόμην is the imperfect passive of τρέφω 'I was being reared'. ὀλίγον δέ τί μ’ ἧσσον ἐτίμα: ὀλίγον τι 'a little', ἧσσον 'less', ἐτίμα the imperfect of τιμάω 'hold in honour', with the mother as subject: she honoured Eumaeus a little less than her own daughter.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἥβην πολυήρατον ἱκόμεθ’ ἄμφω,
τὴν μὲν ἔπειτα Σάμηνδ’ ἔδοσαν καὶ μυρί’ ἕλοντο,
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ hēbēn polyēraton hikometh’ amphō,
tēn men epeita Samēnd’ edosan kai myri’ helonto,
sentences.l:
But when to youth, much-loved, we came, both of us,
her, indeed, then to Same they gave, and numberless things they took,
sentences.i: But when we had both come to beloved youth, they then gave her away to Same, and took countless things,
sentences.n: The unit stops at a comma because the sentence would otherwise run to five lines. ἐπεί ῥ’ is ἐπεὶ ῥα, ῥα being the particle. ἥβην πολυήρατον 'much-loved youth'; ἱκόμεθ’ is the aorist ἱκόμεθα 'we came to', ἄμφω 'both'. Σάμηνδ’ is Σάμην with the suffix -δε of direction, 'to Same', the island. ἔδοσαν 'they gave' (in marriage; the verb needs no object but τὴν μέν 'her'). μυρί’ ἕλοντο: μυρία is 'numberless things', ἕλοντο the aorist middle of αἱρέω 'took for themselves'; the Greek says only 'countless things', probably bride-gifts, but it does not say so.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε εἵματ’ ἐκείνη
καλὰ μάλ’ ἀμφιέσασα, ποσὶν δ’ ὑποδήματα δοῦσα
ἀγρόνδε προΐαλλε·
sentences.tr:
autar eme chlainan te chitōna te heimat’ ekeinē
kala mal’ amphiesasa, posin d’ hypodēmata dousa
agronde proïalle·
sentences.i: But she clothed me in a cloak and tunic, very fine clothes, gave me sandals for my feet, and sent me out to the fields;
sentences.n: Laertes's wife, who reared him, sends the boy out to the country, well dressed. The object of the whole unit is ἐμέ, with ἀμφιέσασα 'having clothed (me)', the aorist participle of ἀμφιέννυμι; what she put on him is χλαῖνα 'cloak', χιτών 'tunic', εἵματα 'clothes', καλὰ μάλ’ 'very fine'. ἐκείνη 'that woman' is the subject. ποσίν is the dative plural of πούς 'foot'; ὑποδήματα 'sandals' are what is bound under the feet; δοῦσα is the aorist participle of δίδωμι. ἀγρόνδε is ἀγρός 'field, country' with the suffix -δε 'to'; προΐαλλε is the imperfect of προϊάλλω 'send forth'.

sentences.t: φίλει δέ με κηρόθι μᾶλλον.
sentences.tr: philei de me kērothi mallon.
sentences.l: and she loved me more in her heart.
sentences.i: and she loved me the more in her heart.
sentences.n: φίλει is the imperfect of φιλέω 'love'. κηρόθι is κῆρ 'heart' with the suffix -θι 'in', so 'in the heart'. μᾶλλον 'more' leaves out what she loved him more than.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἤδη τούτων ἐπιδεύομαι·
sentences.tr: nyn d’ ēdē toutōn epideuomai·
sentences.l: But now already of these things I am in want;
sentences.i: But now I am already in want of all this;
sentences.n: Eumaeus contrasts his present state with the care he once had. ἐπιδεύομαι 'I am in want of, lack' takes the genitive, here τούτων 'of these things', the clothes, sandals and affection just named. νῦν ... ἤδη 'now already'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μοι αὐτῷ
ἔργον ἀέξουσιν μάκαρες θεοὶ ᾧ ἐπιμίμνω·
sentences.tr:
alla moi autōi
ergon aexousin makares theoi hōi epimimnō·
sentences.l:
but for me myself
the work the blessed gods make grow, at which I stay;
sentences.i: but for my own part, the blessed gods make prosper the work I keep at;
sentences.n: ἀλλά 'but': though he lacks those things, his work goes well. αὐτῷ 'myself' strengthens μοι 'for me'. ἔργον ἀέξουσιν 'they make the work grow' (ἀέξω 'increase'); μάκαρες θεοί 'the blessed gods'. ᾧ ἐπιμίμνω 'at which I stay': ᾧ is the relative 'at which' (here not the possessive ὅς), and ἐπιμίμνω is the first singular present of a reduplicated by-form of ἐπιμένω 'stay at, keep to'.

sentences.t: τῶν ἔφαγόν τ’ ἔπιόν τε καὶ αἰδοίοισιν ἔδωκα.
sentences.tr: tōn ephagon t’ epion te kai aidoioisin edōka.
sentences.l: of these I have eaten and drunk, and to revered ones I have given.
sentences.i: From it I have eaten and drunk, and I have given to those who deserve respect.
sentences.n: τῶν 'of these', the genitive of the produce of that work, 'some of it'. ἔφαγον and ἔπιον are aorists; they state what he has done, and does. αἰδοίοισιν is a dative plural in -οισιν, 'to the revered': αἰδοῖος 'revered, held in respect' (from αἰδώς 'respect'), here without a noun, so the Greek says only 'to those who deserve respect'. ἔδωκα 'I gave'.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ἄρα δεσποίνης οὐ μείλιχον ἔστιν ἀκοῦσαι
οὔτ’ ἔπος οὔτε τι ἔργον, ἐπεὶ κακὸν ἔμπεσεν οἴκῳ,
ἄνδρες ὑπερφίαλοι·
sentences.tr:
ek d’ ara despoinēs ou meilichon estin akousai
out’ epos oute ti ergon, epei kakon empesen oikōi,
andres hyperphialoi·
sentences.i: But from the lady of the house there is nothing soothing to be had, in word or in deed, since an evil has fallen on the house, men who are overweening;
sentences.n: The 'lady' is the mistress of the house, Penelope, and the 'overweening men' are the suitors; the text names neither. δέσποινα 'lady, mistress of the household'. οὐ μείλιχον ἔστιν ἀκοῦσαι 'it is not possible to hear anything soothing': ἔστιν with an infinitive means 'it is possible', and μείλιχος is 'soothing, gentle'. ἀκοῦσαι 'to hear' fits ἔπος 'word' better than ἔργον 'deed', and the sense is that no kind word or act comes. ἐπεί 'since'; ἔμπεσεν is the aorist of ἐμπίπτω 'fall upon', with no augment; κακόν 'an evil' is a neuter noun, and ἄνδρες ὑπερφίαλοι 'overweening men' says what it is. ὑπερφίαλος 'overweening' is translated the same wherever it is used of men.

sentences.t:
μέγα δὲ δμῶες χατέουσιν
ἀντία δεσποίνης φάσθαι καὶ ἕκαστα πυθέσθαι
καὶ φαγέμεν πιέμεν τε, ἔπειτα δὲ καί τι φέρεσθαι
ἀγρόνδ’, οἷά τε θυμὸν ἀεὶ δμώεσσιν ἰαίνει.
sentences.tr:
mega de dmōes chateousin
antia despoinēs phasthai kai hekasta pythesthai
kai phagemen piemen te, epeita de kai ti pheresthai
agrond’, hoia te thymon aei dmōessin iainei.
sentences.l:
and greatly servants long
to speak face to face with the lady, and to learn each thing,
and to eat and to drink, and then also something to carry off
to the country, such things as ever the heart for servants warms.”
sentences.i: for servants greatly long to speak to the lady face to face and to hear about everything, to eat and drink, and then to take something away with them to the country, the kind of thing that always warms a servant's heart.”
sentences.n: The four infinitives φάσθαι, πυθέσθαι, φαγέμεν πιέμεν and φέρεσθαι all depend on χατέουσιν 'long for, have need of' (δμῶες 'servants'). φάσθαι is the middle infinitive of φημί 'speak'; πυθέσθαι the aorist infinitive of πυνθάνομαι 'learn'; φαγέμεν and πιέμεν are infinitives in -έμεν (Attic -εῖν), 'to eat' and 'to drink'. ἀντία δεσποίνης 'face to face with the lady'; ἕκαστα 'each thing, every detail'. φέρεσθαι is the middle, 'carry off for oneself'; ἀγρόνδ’ is 'to the country' (suffix -δε). οἷα is 'such things as', with ἰαίνει 'warms, gladdens'; a neuter plural subject takes a singular verb, and θυμόν 'heart' is the object.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē polymētis Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: Odysseus, still in disguise, replies to Eumaeus's story. This is a whole-line reply formula: ἀπαμειβόμενος 'answering', προσέφη 'addressed' (aorist of πρόσφημι), πολύμητις 'of many wiles', from μῆτις 'cunning intelligence'. The epithet is translated every time, even where no cunning is in view.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, ὡς ἄρα τυτθὸς ἐών, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα,
πολλὸν ἀπεπλάγχθης σῆς πατρίδος ἠδὲ τοκήων.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, hōs ara tytthos eōn, Eumaie sybōta,
pollon apeplanchthēs sēs patridos ēde tokēōn.
sentences.l:
“Ah! how, then, so small being, Eumaeus swineherd,
far you were driven away from your fatherland and your parents.
sentences.i: “Ah, how far you were driven from your fatherland and your parents, Eumaeus the swineherd, when you were so small!
sentences.n: Odysseus reacts to what Eumaeus has said of his upbringing. ὢ πόποι is the exclamation 'Ah!'; ὡς ἄρα makes the sentence an exclamation, 'how, then'. τυτθός 'little' with ἐών, the epic participle of εἰμί 'being', is 'when you were small'. Εὔμαιε συβῶτα are both vocatives, συβῶτα being the Ionic vocative of συβώτης. ἀπεπλάγχθης is the aorist passive of ἀποπλάζω 'drive off course', the verb of πλάγχθη in the proem (1.2). πολλόν 'far'. σῆς πατρίδος is a genitive of separation, 'from your fatherland', and τοκήων is the genitive plural of τοκῆες 'parents'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι τόδε εἰπὲ καὶ ἀτρεκέως κατάλεξον,
ἠὲ διεπράθετο πτόλις ἀνδρῶν εὐρυάγυια,
ᾗ ἔνι ναιετάασκε πατὴρ καὶ πότνια μήτηρ,
sentences.tr:
all’ age moi tode eipe kai atrekeōs katalexon,
ēe diepratheto ptolis andrōn euryaguia,
hēi eni naietaaske patēr kai potnia mētēr,
sentences.l:
But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly,
whether was sacked the city of men, wide-streeted,
in which used to dwell a father and a lady mother,
sentences.i: But come now, tell me this, and set it out for me exactly: whether the city of men with its wide streets was sacked, where your father and lady mother lived,
sentences.n: Odysseus puts his guesses to Eumaeus as two alternatives, ἠέ ... ἦ 'whether ... or whether'; this unit holds the first, and it stops at the comma that divides them. The first line is the fixed formula 'But come, tell me this, and recount it exactly': ἀλλ’ ἄγε 'but come', ἀτρεκέως 'exactly', κατάλεξον the aorist imperative of καταλέγω 'recount'. διεπράθετο is the aorist middle of διαπέρθω 'sack', with passive sense, 'was sacked'. πτόλις is the epic form of πόλις. εὐρυάγυια 'with wide streets' joins εὐρύς 'wide' to ἀγυιά 'street'. ᾗ ἔνι is ἐν ᾗ 'in which', the preposition standing after the relative pronoun; ναιετάασκε is the iterative imperfect of ναιετάω, 'used to dwell'.

sentences.t:
ἦ σέ γε μουνωθέντα παρ’ οἴεσιν ἢ παρὰ βουσὶν
ἄνδρες δυσμενέες νηυσὶν λάβον ἠδ’ ἐπέρασσαν
τοῦδ’ ἀνδρὸς πρὸς δώμαθ’, ὁ δ’ ἄξιον ὦνον ἔδωκε.
sentences.tr:
ē se ge mounōthenta par’ oiesin ē para bousin
andres dysmenees nēusin labon ēd’ eperassan
toud’ andros pros dōmath’, ho d’ axion ōnon edōke.
sentences.l:
or you, indeed, left alone beside sheep or beside cattle,
ill-disposed men with ships seized, and sold
to this man's house, and he gave a worthy price.”
sentences.i: or whether, when you were left alone with the sheep or the cattle, ill-disposed men took you off in ships and sold you to this man's house, and he paid a fair price.”
sentences.n: The second alternative: Odysseus guesses that Eumaeus was kidnapped and sold into service. ἦ ... ἢ ... is 'or whether ... or'. σέ ... μουνωθέντα 'you, left alone' is the aorist passive participle of μουνόω; οἴεσιν is a dative plural of ὄις 'sheep', and βουσίν of βοῦς 'cattle'. δυσμενέες 'ill-disposed' (δυσμενής); νηυσίν is the dative plural of ναῦς, 'with ships'. λάβον is the aorist of λαμβάνω with no augment, and ἐπέρασσαν is the aorist of περάω, 'carried abroad and sold'. τοῦδ’ ἀνδρός 'this man's': ὅδε is the 'this here' demonstrative, and no man is named. δώμαθ’ is δώματα. The last clause ὁ δ’ ἄξιον ὦνον ἔδωκε 'and he paid a fair price' (ἄξιον 'worth, matching in worth', ὦνον 'price') returns word for word at 429.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε συβώτης, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe sybōtēs, orchamos andrōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the swineherd, chief of men:
sentences.i: Then the swineherd, chief of men, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at 351, and the same English.

sentences.t:
ξεῖν’, ἐπεὶ ἂρ δὴ ταῦτά μ’ ἀνείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς,
σιγῇ νῦν ξυνίει καὶ τέρπεο, πῖνέ τε οἶνον
ἥμενος.
sentences.tr:
xein’, epei ar dē tauta m’ aneireai ēde metallāis,
sigēi nyn xyniei kai terpeo, pine te oinon
hēmenos.
sentences.l:
“Stranger, since indeed you ask me these things and inquire,
in silence now attend and take your pleasure, and drink wine
sitting.
sentences.i: “Stranger, since you do ask me this and inquire into it, listen now in silence and enjoy yourself, and drink your wine as you sit there.
sentences.n: Eumaeus does not answer the question yet; he first tells Odysseus to settle down for a long evening. ξεῖν’ is ξεῖνε 'stranger'; ἐπεὶ ἂρ δή is 'since indeed' (ἂρ being the particle ἄρα). ἀνείρεαι is the uncontracted second singular of ἀνείρομαι 'ask' (Attic ἀνείρῃ), and μεταλλᾷς the contracted second singular of μεταλλάω 'inquire'. σιγῇ 'in silence' is a dative; ξυνίει is the imperative of συνίημι 'attend, give heed' (ξυν- is συν-); τέρπεο is the imperative middle of τέρπω 'take your pleasure'; πῖνε is the imperative of πίνω; ἥμενος 'sitting' is the participle of ἧμαι.

sentences.t: αἵδε δὲ νύκτες ἀθέσφατοι·
sentences.tr: haide de nyktes athesphatoi·
sentences.l: and these nights are immense;
sentences.i: These nights are immense;
sentences.n: αἵδε is the feminine nominative plural of ὅδε 'this here', agreeing with νύκτες 'nights'. ἀθέσφατος 'immense' is a word whose sense is not certain: it is built on ἀ- and θέσφατος 'god-declared', and 'unspeakable, immense' is the traditional reading.

sentences.t:
ἔστι μὲν εὕδειν,
ἔστι δὲ τερπομένοισιν ἀκούειν·
sentences.tr:
esti men heudein,
esti de terpomenoisin akouein·
sentences.l:
it is possible, indeed, to sleep,
it is possible for those taking pleasure to listen;
sentences.i: you may sleep, and those who are taking their pleasure may listen;
sentences.n: ἔστι with an infinitive means 'it is possible': ἔστι μὲν εὕδειν 'one may sleep', ἔστι δὲ ... ἀκούειν 'one may listen', the μέν and δέ setting the two options side by side. τερπομένοισιν is the dative plural participle of τέρπομαι 'take pleasure', 'for those who enjoy it'.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί σε χρή,
πρὶν ὥρη, καταλέχθαι·
sentences.tr:
oude ti se chrē,
prin hōrē, katalechthai·
sentences.l:
and not at all is it needful for you,
before the hour, to lie down;
sentences.i: and there is no need at all for you to lie down before it is time;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τί σε χρή 'nor is there any need for you': χρή 'it is necessary', τι 'at all'. πρὶν ὥρη 'before the hour', that is before it is time; ὥρη is 'the proper time', with a verb 'is' left out. καταλέχθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of καταλέγω 'lie down'.

sentences.t: ἀνίη καὶ πολὺς ὕπνος.
sentences.tr: aniē kai polys hypnos.
sentences.l: an irksomeness, even much sleep.
sentences.i: even a great deal of sleep is tiresome.
sentences.n: ἀνίη is a noun, 'irksomeness, vexation' (the family of ἀνιάομαι 'be distressed'); the Greek has no verb, 'a vexation, even much sleep'. καί 'even', πολὺς ὕπνος 'much sleep'.

sentences.t:
τῶν δ’ ἄλλων ὅτινα κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀνώγει,
εὑδέτω ἐξελθών·
sentences.tr:
tōn d’ allōn hotina kradiē kai thymos anōgei,
heudetō exelthōn·
sentences.l:
And of the others, whomever heart and spirit urge,
let him sleep, having gone out;
sentences.i: As for the others, let whoever feels the urging of heart and spirit go out and sleep;
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων is a genitive of the group, 'of the others'; ὅτινα is ὅν τινα 'whomever'. κραδίη καὶ θυμός 'heart and spirit': the two words stand together, so θυμός is 'spirit' to keep them apart. ἀνώγει 'urges' is a present-sense form of the verb ἄνωγα 'bid, urge', whose basic forms are perfect. εὑδέτω is the third singular imperative of εὕδω 'sleep', 'let him sleep', and ἐξελθών 'having gone out' (of the hut).

sentences.t:
ἅμα δ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι
δειπνήσας ἅμ’ ὕεσσιν ἀνακτορίῃσιν ἑπέσθω.
sentences.tr:
hama d’ ēoi phainomenēphi
deipnēsas ham’ hyessin anaktoriēisin hepesthō.
sentences.l:
and with dawn appearing
having eaten his meal, with the lord's pigs let him follow.
sentences.i: and when dawn appears, let him eat his meal and go along with the lord's pigs.
sentences.n: ἅμα δ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι 'and at dawn's appearing': ἠοῖ is the dative of ἠώς 'dawn', and φαινομένηφι has the old ending -φι, which later Greek lost. δειπνήσας 'having taken his meal' (δεῖπνον). ἅμ’ ὕεσσιν ἀνακτορίῃσιν 'along with the lord's pigs': ὕεσσιν is the dative plural of ὗς 'pig', and ἀνακτορίῃσιν is a rare adjective built on ἄναξ 'lord', 'belonging to the lord', the swineherd's master. ἑπέσθω is the aorist imperative of ἕπομαι 'follow'.

sentences.t:
νῶϊ δ’ ἐνὶ κλισίῃ πίνοντέ τε δαινυμένω τε
κήδεσιν ἀλλήλων τερπώμεθα λευγαλέοισι,
μνωομένω·
sentences.tr:
nōï d’ eni klisiēi pinonte te dainymenō te
kēdesin allēlōn terpōmetha leugaleoisi,
mnōomenō·
sentences.i: and let the two of us, in the hut, drinking and feasting, take our pleasure in each other's pitiful sorrows as we call them to mind;
sentences.n: νῶϊ is the dual 'we two' (Eumaeus and Odysseus), and the participles πίνοντε, δαινυμένω and μνωομένω are dual as well. ἐνὶ κλισίῃ 'in the hut'. τερπώμεθα is the present subjunctive in an exhortation, 'let us take pleasure', with the dative κήδεσιν ἀλλήλων λευγαλέοισι 'in each other's pitiful sorrows' (κῆδος 'sorrow', λευγαλέος 'pitiful'). μνωομένω is the uncontracted form of μνάομαι 'remember, call to mind' (Attic μνωμένω).

sentences.t:
μετὰ γάρ τε καὶ ἄλγεσι τέρπεται ἀνήρ,
ὅς τις δὴ μάλα πολλὰ πάθῃ καὶ πόλλ’ ἐπαληθῇ.
sentences.tr:
meta gar te kai algesi terpetai anēr,
hos tis dē mala polla pathēi kai poll’ epalēthēi.
sentences.l:
for afterwards even in pains takes pleasure a man,
whoever very much has suffered and much has wandered.
sentences.i: for afterwards a man takes pleasure even in his pains, whoever has suffered very much and wandered much.
sentences.n: This is the reason for the plan, stated as a general truth: γάρ τε, with the epic τε that marks such truths. μετά is read as the adverb 'afterwards' (it could also be taken with ἄλγεσι 'among pains'). τέρπεται 'takes pleasure', ἄλγεσι 'in pains', dative of ἄλγος. ὅς τις δή is 'whoever indeed', with the aorist subjunctives πάθῃ 'has suffered' and ἐπαληθῇ 'has wandered', the second the aorist passive of ἐπαλάομαι 'wander about'; πόλλ’ is πολλά, 'many things' with πάθῃ and 'much' (adverbial) with ἐπαληθῇ.

sentences.t: τοῦτο δέ τοι ἐρέω ὅ μ’ ἀνείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς.
sentences.tr: touto de toi ereō ho m’ aneireai ēde metallāis.
sentences.l: but this to you I will tell, which me you ask and inquire after.
sentences.i: But this I will tell you, what you ask me and inquire after.
sentences.n: Eumaeus now promises the answer that has been asked of him. τοῦτο 'this', τοι 'to you', ἐρέω 'I will tell', ὅ 'what, which'. ἀνείρεαι ἠδὲ μεταλλᾷς repeats 390, 'you ask and inquire'.

sentences.t:
νῆσός τις Συρίη κικλήσκεται, εἴ που ἀκούεις,
Ὀρτυγίης καθύπερθεν, ὅθι τροπαὶ ἠελίοιο,
οὔ τι περιπληθὴς λίην τόσον, ἀλλ’ ἀγαθὴ μέν,
εὔβοτος, εὔμηλος, οἰνοπληθής, πολύπυρος.
sentences.tr:
nēsos tis Syriē kiklēsketai, ei pou akoueis,
Ortygiēs kathyperthen, hothi tropai ēelioio,
ou ti periplēthēs liēn toson, all’ agathē men,
eubotos, eumēlos, oinoplēthēs, polypyros.
sentences.l:
A certain island, Syrie, is called, if perhaps you have heard,
above Ortygia, where are the turnings of the sun,
not at all very populous, so very much, but good, indeed,
good-grazing, well-flocked, wine-abounding, rich in wheat.
sentences.i: There is an island called Syrie, if you have ever heard of it, above Ortygia, where the sun turns; it is not at all so very populous, but it is a good land, good for grazing, rich in flocks, abounding in wine, rich in wheat.
sentences.n: The story of Eumaeus's birth begins on an island. Συρίη is the Ionic form of Συρία, but this is not the later country of Syria; where the island lay is not known. κικλήσκεται 'is called' is the reduplicated present of καλέω; εἴ που ἀκούεις 'if you have heard of it anywhere'. Ὀρτυγίης καθύπερθεν 'above Ortygia', a genitive after the preposition. τροπαὶ ἠελίοιο 'the turnings of the sun' was explained in more than one way, and the meaning is not certain. οὔ τι περιπληθὴς λίην τόσον 'not at all so very populous' (περιπληθής 'very full, crowded'). Four adjectives follow: εὔβοτος 'good for grazing' (εὖ + βόσκω), εὔμηλος 'rich in flocks', οἰνοπληθής 'abounding in wine', πολύπυρος 'rich in wheat'. Συρίη and Ὀρτυγίης show Ionic η where Attic has long α, and ἠελίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου).

sentences.t:
πείνη δ’ οὔ ποτε δῆμον ἐσέρχεται, οὐδέ τις ἄλλη
νοῦσος ἐπὶ στυγερὴ πέλεται δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
peinē d’ ou pote dēmon eserchetai, oude tis allē
nousos epi stygerē peletai deiloisi brotoisin·
sentences.l:
And hunger never enters the land, nor any other
sickness, hateful, comes upon miserable mortals;
sentences.i: Hunger never enters the land, nor does any other hateful sickness come upon miserable mortals;
sentences.n: πείνη 'hunger' (Attic πεῖνα); δῆμος 'land'; ἐσέρχεται 'enters'. νοῦσος 'sickness' is the epic form of νόσος; στυγερή 'hateful'. ἐπὶ ... πέλεται 'comes upon' has its preverb ἐπί standing apart from the verb (tmesis). δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσιν is a dative plural in -οισι(ν), 'to miserable mortals'; δειλός 'miserable' and βροτός 'mortal'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε γηράσκωσι πόλιν κάτα φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων,
ἐλθὼν ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων Ἀρτέμιδι ξὺν
οἷς ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν ἐποιχόμενος κατέπεφνεν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote gēraskōsi polin kata phyl’ anthrōpōn,
elthōn argyrotoxos Apollōn Artemidi xyn
hois aganois beleessin epoichomenos katepephnen.
sentences.l:
but when the tribes of men grow old throughout the city,
having come, silver-bowed Apollo, with Artemis together,
with his own gentle shafts assailing, slew.
sentences.i: But when the tribes of men grow old in the city, silver-bowed Apollo comes with Artemis, assails them with his gentle arrows, and kills them.
sentences.n: People on this island die old and without sickness, killed by the gods' arrows. ἀλλ’ ὅτε γηράσκωσι 'but when they grow old' has the subjunctive of a general clause, 'whenever'. πόλιν κάτα is κατὰ πόλιν 'throughout the city', the preposition after its noun; φῦλ’ ἀνθρώπων 'tribes of men'. ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων 'silver-bowed Apollo'; Ἀρτέμιδι ξύν is σὺν Ἀρτέμιδι 'with Artemis'. οἷς is the possessive 'his own' (not the relative); ἀγανοῖς βελέεσσιν 'with gentle shafts' is a dative plural in -εσσιν, and ἀγανός 'gentle' suggests that the death is gentle (traditionally sudden and painless). ἐποιχόμενος 'going against, assailing'. κατέπεφνεν 'killed' is an aorist used for what always happens, so the plain-English layer uses the present.

sentences.t: ἔνθα δύω πόλιες, δίχα δέ σφισι πάντα δέδασται·
sentences.tr: entha dyō polies, dicha de sphisi panta dedastai·
sentences.l: There two cities, and in two parts for them all has been divided;
sentences.i: There are two cities, and everything there has been divided in two between them;
sentences.n: ἔνθα 'there'; δύω is δύο 'two'; πόλιες is the epic plural of πόλις (Attic πόλεις). δίχα 'in two'; σφισι is the dative plural of the pronoun, 'for them'; δέδασται is the perfect passive of δατέομαι 'divide', 'has been divided'.

sentences.t:
τῇσιν δ’ ἀμφοτέρῃσι πατὴρ ἐμὸς ἐμβασίλευε,
Κτήσιος Ὀρμενίδης, ἐπιείκελος ἀθανάτοισιν.
sentences.tr:
tēisin d’ amphoterēisi patēr emos embasileue,
Ktēsios Ormenidēs, epieikelos athanatoisin.
sentences.l:
and over them both my father reigned,
Ctesius, Ormenus' son, resembling the immortals.
sentences.i: Over both of them my father was king: Ctesius, son of Ormenus, like the immortals.
sentences.n: Eumaeus tells his own origin: he is a king's son. τῇσιν ἀμφοτέρῃσι 'over both of them': τῇσιν is the pronoun in the dative plural with the ending -ῃσιν. πατὴρ ἐμός 'my father'; ἐμβασίλευε 'was king in' is the imperfect of ἐμβασιλεύω. Κτήσιος Ὀρμενίδης 'Ctesius, son of Ormenus': -ίδης is the patronymic ending. ἐπιείκελος ἀθανάτοισιν 'resembling the immortals' is a stock epithet, and is translated even though it is used here of a man in a story.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ Φοίνικες ναυσίκλυτοι ἤλυθον ἄνδρες,
τρῶκται, μυρί’ ἄγοντες ἀθύρματα νηῒ μελαίνῃ.
sentences.tr:
entha de Phoinikes nausiklytoi ēlython andres,
trōktai, myri’ agontes athyrmata nēï melainēi.
sentences.l:
And there Phoenicians, ship-famous men, came,
gnawers, countless playthings bringing in a black ship.
sentences.i: And there came Phoenician men, famous for their ships, rogues, bringing countless trinkets in a black ship.
sentences.n: Phoenicians, the sea-traders of the Levantine coast, arrive. ἤλυθον is ἦλθον 'came'. ναυσίκλυτοι 'ship-famous' is ναῦς 'ship' with κλυτός 'famous'. τρῶκται is the plural of τρώκτης, from τρώγω 'gnaw'; its sense is not secure, and 'rogues' is taken from the context. μυρί’ ἀθύρματα 'countless playthings': ἀθύρματα are 'toys, trinkets', from ἀθύρω 'play'. νηῒ μελαίνῃ is the dative of ναῦς, 'in a black ship'.

sentences.t:
ἔσκε δὲ πατρὸς ἐμοῖο γυνὴ Φοίνισσ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
καλή τε μεγάλη τε καὶ ἀγλαὰ ἔργα ἰδυῖα·
sentences.tr:
eske de patros emoio gynē Phoiniss’ eni oikōi,
kalē te megalē te kai aglaa erga iduia·
sentences.l:
And there was of my father a woman, Phoenician, in the house,
fine and tall and knowing splendid works;
sentences.i: My father had in his house a Phoenician woman, beautiful and tall, and skilled in splendid handiwork;
sentences.n: This woman is the one whom the Phoenicians will deceive. ἔσκε is the iterative imperfect of εἰμί 'was'. γυνή is simply 'woman'; her standing in the household is not stated. πατρὸς ἐμοῖο 'of my father' is a genitive in -οιο (Attic -ου). Φοίνισσ’ is Φοίνισσα 'Phoenician woman', and ἐνὶ οἴκῳ 'in the house'. καλή τε μεγάλη τε 'fine and tall' (μεγάλη 'big', of a person 'tall'). ἀγλαὰ ἔργα ἰδυῖα 'knowing splendid works': ἰδυῖα is the feminine perfect participle of οἶδα, 'knowing, skilled', and ἔργα 'works' are here a woman's handiwork.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἄρα Φοίνικες πολυπαίπαλοι ἠπερόπευον.
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ara Phoinikes polypaipaloi ēperopeuon.
sentences.l: Her then the Phoenicians, very-artful, were deceiving.
sentences.i: And the very artful Phoenicians set about deceiving her.
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἄρα 'her then'. πολυπαίπαλοι 'very artful' is a rare epithet of the Phoenicians; its sense is not certain, and 'very artful' is the traditional guess. ἠπερόπευον is the imperfect of ἠπεροπεύω 'deceive, cheat', the verb that comes back at 421.

sentences.t:
πλυνούσῃ τις πρῶτα μίγη κοίλῃ παρὰ νηῒ
εὐνῇ καὶ φιλότητι, τά τε φρένας ἠπεροπεύει
θηλυτέρῃσι γυναιξί, καὶ ἥ κ’ εὐεργὸς ἔῃσιν.
sentences.tr:
plynousēi tis prōta migē koilēi para nēï
eunēi kai philotēti, ta te phrenas ēperopeuei
thēlyterēisi gynaixi, kai hē k’ euergos eēisin.
sentences.l:
As she was washing, someone first was mingled with her, beside the hollow ship,
in bed and in love, which the wits deceives
for female women, even whichever may be well-working.
sentences.i: As she was washing beside the hollow ship, one of them first lay with her in bed and in love, things that deceive the wits of women, even of one who does well.
sentences.n: This is how the deceit begins. πλυνούσῃ is the dative participle of πλύνω 'wash', 'to her as she washed', and μίγη is the aorist passive of μίγνυμι, 'was mingled with', taking a dative. τις 'someone', that is one of the Phoenicians; πρῶτα 'first'. κοίλῃ παρὰ νηῒ 'beside the hollow ship'. εὐνῇ καὶ φιλότητι 'in bed and in love' are datives. τά τε φρένας ἠπεροπεύει θηλυτέρῃσι γυναιξί: τά is 'which' referring to bed and love (a neuter plural with a singular verb), τε the epic particle of a general truth, φρένας 'the wits', θηλυτέρῃσι γυναιξί 'for women'. καὶ ἥ κ’ εὐεργὸς ἔῃσιν 'even one who may be εὐεργός': εὐεργός means 'well-working, doing well', and whether it means skilled or upright is left open; ἔῃσιν is the epic subjunctive of εἰμί, with κε.

sentences.t: εἰρώτα δὴ ἔπειτα τίς εἴη καὶ πόθεν ἔλθοι·
sentences.tr: eirōta dē epeita tis eiē kai pothen elthoi·
sentences.l: He asked then who she might be and from where she came;
sentences.i: Then he asked her who she was and where she had come from;
sentences.n: εἰρώτα is the imperfect of εἰρωτάω (the same verb as ἐρωτάω) 'ask'. τίς εἴη καὶ πόθεν ἔλθοι is an indirect question with the optative after a verb in the past, 'who she was and whence she came'. The subject is the Phoenician of the previous unit.

sentences.t: ἡ δὲ μάλ’ αὐτίκα πατρὸς ἐπέφραδεν ὑψερεφὲς δῶ·
sentences.tr: hē de mal’ autika patros epephraden hypserephes dō·
sentences.l: And she very promptly of her father pointed out the high-roofed house.
sentences.i: And she at once pointed out her father’s high-roofed house.
sentences.n: ἐπέφραδεν is the aorist of φράζω 'point out, show'. ὑψερεφὲς δῶ 'high-roofed house' (δῶ is the short form of δῶμα). πατρός is bare 'of the father': the Greek has no possessive and does not say whose father, and the English keeps the wording already fixed for this line. μάλ’ αὐτίκα 'very promptly'.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μὲν Σιδῶνος πολυχάλκου εὔχομαι εἶναι,
κούρη δ’ εἴμ’ Ἀρύβαντος ἐγὼ ῥυδὸν ἀφνειοῖο·
sentences.tr:
ek men Sidōnos polychalkou euchomai einai,
kourē d’ eim’ Arybantos egō rhydon aphneioio·
sentences.l:
‘From Sidon, indeed, rich in bronze, I declare myself to be,
and daughter I am, I, of Arybas, in a flood rich;
sentences.i: ‘I declare that I am from Sidon, rich in bronze, and I am the daughter of Arybas, who is overflowingly rich;
sentences.n: From here to the end of the part Eumaeus quotes what the woman and the Phoenician said, so these speeches have single quotation marks inside his own. She answers the Phoenician's question. Σιδών is Sidon, a Phoenician city, and πολύχαλκος 'rich in bronze' is a compound of the kind of πολύχρυσος 'rich in gold'. εὔχομαι εἶναι 'I declare myself to be': εὔχομαι is 'pray' or 'declare, claim', and the second sense is meant. κούρη 'daughter'; Ἀρύβαντος 'of Arybas'. ῥυδόν is a rare adverb, probably from ῥέω 'flow', 'in a flood, abundantly', and its exact sense is not certain; ἀφνειοῖο 'rich' is a genitive in -οιο agreeing with Ἀρύβαντος.

sentences.t:
ἀλλά μ’ ἀνήρπαξαν Τάφιοι ληΐστορες ἄνδρες
ἀγρόθεν ἐρχομένην, πέρασαν δέ τε δεῦρ’ ἀγαγόντες
τοῦδ’ ἀνδρὸς πρὸς δώμαθ’·
sentences.tr:
alla m’ anērpaxan Taphioi lēïstores andres
agrothen erchomenēn, perasan de te deur’ agagontes
toud’ andros pros dōmath’·
sentences.i: but Taphian raiders snatched me away as I was coming from the fields, and brought me here and sold me to this man's house;
sentences.n: She tells of her capture. ἀνήρπαξαν is the aorist of ἀναρπάζω 'snatch away'. Τάφιοι ληΐστορες ἄνδρες 'Taphian raiders': the Taphians are the people of Taphos, and ληΐστωρ 'raider' comes from ληΐς 'spoil'. ἀγρόθεν 'from the field', with the suffix -θεν 'from'; ἐρχομένην is a feminine participle agreeing with μ’, 'as I came'. πέρασαν is ἐπέρασαν, the aorist of περάω 'carry abroad and sell', without the augment; δέ τε are particles; δεῦρ’ 'here'; ἀγαγόντες 'having led'. τοῦδ’ ἀνδρὸς πρὸς δώμαθ’ 'to this man's house': τοῦδε points to a man at hand, and he is not named.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἄξιον ὦνον ἔδωκε.
sentences.tr: ho d’ axion ōnon edōke.
sentences.l: and he gave a worthy price.’
sentences.i: and he paid a fair price.’
sentences.n: The same words as at 388: ὁ is the pronoun 'he', ἄξιον 'worth, matching in worth', ὦνον 'price' (accusative). Here they close the woman's account of how she came to the house.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν ἀνήρ, ὃς ἐμίσγετο λάθρη·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipen anēr, hos emisgeto lathrē·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the man who was mingling with her in secret:
sentences.i: Then the man who was lying with her in secret spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: A reply formula in which the speaker is named by what he does: ἀνήρ, ὃς ἐμίσγετο λάθρη 'the man who was mingling with her in secret'. ἐμίσγετο is the imperfect of μίσγω, the same verb as μίγη at 420, and λάθρη 'secretly'; he seems to be the man of 420. τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν 'her then in turn addressed' is the formula of 351 with τήν, for a woman addressed.

sentences.l:
‘Would you then now back again with us homeward follow,
so that you may see of father and mother the high-roofed house
and themselves?
sentences.i: ‘Would you now come back again with us to your home, so that you might see the high-roofed house of your father and mother, and themselves too?
sentences.n: The Phoenician offers to take her home: this is the bait. ἦ ῥά κε ... ἕποιο 'would you then ... follow': ἦ ῥα opens a question, κε with the optative ἕποιο (ἕπομαι 'follow') makes it 'would you'. πάλιν αὖτις 'back again' is a doubled adverb; ἅμ’ ἡμῖν 'along with us'; οἴκαδ’ 'homeward' (suffix -δε). ὄφρα ἴδῃ 'so that you may see' is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive of εἶδον. ὑψερεφὲς δῶ 'high-roofed house'. αὐτούς τ’ is 'and themselves', the parents; the question mark of the Greek (;) falls here.

sentences.t: ἦ γὰρ ἔτ’ εἰσὶ καὶ ἀφνειοὶ καλέονται.
sentences.tr: ē gar et’ eisi kai aphneioi kaleontai.
sentences.l: for indeed they are still, and rich they are called.’
sentences.i: for they are still alive, and they are called rich.’
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ 'for indeed'; ἔτ’ εἰσί 'they are still (alive)'; ἀφνειοί 'rich'; καλέονται is the uncontracted passive 'are called' (Attic καλοῦνται). The man gives a reason for her to go home, to see parents who still live and are wealthy.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε γυνὴ καὶ ἀμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe gynē kai ameibeto mythōi·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed the woman, and answered with a word:
sentences.i: Then the woman spoke to him in turn, and answered him:
sentences.n: Another reply formula, with a second verb added: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε 'him then in turn addressed' and καὶ ἀμείβετο μύθῳ 'and answered with a word'. ἀμείβετο is ἠμείβετο without the augment, and μύθῳ is a dative, 'with a word' (μῦθος 'word, speech'). γυνή is 'woman', the Phoenician woman.

sentences.t:
εἴη κεν καὶ τοῦτ’, εἴ μοι ἐθέλοιτέ γε, ναῦται,
ὅρκῳ πιστωθῆναι ἀπήμονά μ’ οἴκαδ’ ἀπάξειν.
sentences.tr:
eiē ken kai tout’, ei moi etheloite ge, nautai,
horkōi pistōthēnai apēmona m’ oikad’ apaxein.
sentences.l:
‘This too might be, if to me you were willing, at least, sailors,
by oath to be pledged to take me unharmed homeward.’
sentences.i: ‘That could be done too, if you sailors were willing to bind yourselves by an oath to take me home unharmed.’
sentences.n: She agrees, on a condition. εἴη κεν καὶ τοῦτ’ 'this too might be (possible)': κεν is the epic form of κε, and the optative with it gives 'might'. εἴ μοι ἐθέλοιτέ γε, ναῦται 'if you were willing, sailors, for me': ἐθέλοιτε is the second plural optative. ὅρκῳ πιστωθῆναι 'to be pledged by an oath' is the aorist passive infinitive of πιστόω 'make trustworthy, bind'. ἀπήμονά μ’ οἴκαδ’ ἀπάξειν 'to take me home unharmed': ἀπάξειν is the future infinitive of ἀπάγω, and ἀπήμων 'unharmed' here of a person.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπώμνυον ὡς ἐκέλευεν.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes epōmnyon hōs ekeleuen.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and they then, all of them, swore as she bade.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and they all swore as she told them to.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’ 'so she spoke' is the usual closing formula for a speech, here after a woman's; ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο elided before the rough breathing of οἱ. ἐπώμνυον is the imperfect of ἐπομνύω 'swear to it', 'they swore'; ὡς ἐκέλευεν 'as she bade' (κελεύω).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὄμοσάν τε τελεύτησάν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
τοῖς δ’ αὖτις μετέειπε γυνὴ καὶ ἀμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ omosan te teleutēsan te ton horkon,
tois d’ autis meteeipe gynē kai ameibeto mythōi·
sentences.l:
But when then they had sworn and completed the oath,
then among them again spoke the woman, and answered with a word:
sentences.i: When they had sworn and completed the oath, the woman spoke among them again, and answered:
sentences.n: ὄμοσαν is the aorist of ὄμνυμι 'swear' and τελεύτησαν the aorist of τελευτάω 'complete'; ῥ’ is ῥα. τοῖς δ’ αὖτις μετέειπε 'and among them again spoke': μετέειπε 'spoke among', αὖτις 'again'. γυνὴ καὶ ἀμείβετο μύθῳ is the formula of 434, 'the woman, and answered with a word'; no one has just spoken to her, so ἀμείβετο means only that she speaks on.

sentences.t:
σιγῇ νῦν, μή τίς με προσαυδάτω ἐπέεσσιν
ὑμετέρων ἑτάρων, ξυμβλήμενος ἢ ἐν ἀγυιῇ,
ἤ που ἐπὶ κρήνῃ·
sentences.tr:
sigēi nyn, mē tis me prosaudatō epeessin
hymeterōn hetarōn, xymblēmenos ē en aguiēi,
ē pou epi krēnēi·
sentences.i: ‘Be silent now: let none of your companions speak to me when he meets me, whether in the street or perhaps at the spring;
sentences.n: She now sets her terms of secrecy. σιγῇ νῦν 'in silence now'. μή τίς με προσαυδάτω ἐπέεσσιν 'let no one speak to me with words': μή with a third person imperative forbids, προσαυδάτω is from προσαυδάω 'speak to', and ἐπέεσσιν is the dative plural of ἔπος 'word'. ὑμετέρων ἑτάρων 'of your companions' is partitive. ξυμβλήμενος is συμβλήμενος 'meeting (me)', the aorist middle participle of συμβάλλω. ἀγυιῇ 'street', κρήνῃ 'spring' are datives; ἤ ... ἤ 'either ... or', with που 'perhaps'.

sentences.t:
μή τις ποτὶ δῶμα γέροντι
ἐλθὼν ἐξείπῃ, ὁ δ’ ὀϊσάμενος καταδήσῃ
δεσμῷ ἐν ἀργαλέῳ, ὑμῖν δ’ ἐπιφράσσετ’ ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr:
mē tis poti dōma geronti
elthōn exeipēi, ho d’ oïsamenos katadēsēi
desmōi en argaleōi, hymin d’ epiphrasset’ olethron.
sentences.l:
lest someone to the house, to the old man,
going, tell, and he, suspecting, bind me
in a grievous bond, and for you devise destruction.
sentences.i: lest anyone go to the old man at the house and tell him, and he, suspecting it, bind me in a grievous bond and plan destruction for you.
sentences.n: The reason for the silence: μή τις ... ἐξείπῃ ... καταδήσῃ 'lest anyone tell ... and he bind', with subjunctives after μή. ποτὶ δῶμα γέροντι 'to the house, to the old man': ποτί is πρός, and γέροντι is the dative of γέρων 'old man', the master of the house. ἐλθών 'going'; ἐξείπῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἐξεῖπον 'tell out'. ὀϊσάμενος 'suspecting' is the aorist middle participle of ὀΐω. καταδήσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of καταδέω 'bind fast' (its object, 'me', is understood), and δεσμῷ ἐν ἀργαλέῳ 'in a grievous bond'. ἐπιφράσσετ’ is ἐπιφράσσεται elided, a short-vowel subjunctive of ἐπιφράζομαι 'plan against', with ὑμῖν 'against you'. ὄλεθρον 'destruction'.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔχετ’ ἐν φρεσὶ μῦθον, ἐπείγετε δ’ ὦνον ὁδαίων.
sentences.tr: all’ echet’ en phresi mython, epeigete d’ ōnon hodaiōn.
sentences.l: But keep in your minds the word, and hasten the purchase of road-goods.
sentences.i: But keep this word in your minds, and hurry on the buying of goods for the journey.
sentences.n: ἔχετ’ ἐν φρεσὶ μῦθον 'keep the word in your minds': ἔχετε is the imperative of ἔχω, φρεσί the dative plural of φρήν, μῦθον 'word, matter'. ἐπείγετε 'press on, hasten'. ὦνον ὁδαίων 'the purchase of goods for the road': ὦνος is 'price' (as at 388, 429) and 'purchase', and ὁδαῖα is a rare word, 'things for the road', whose exact sense here is not certain.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε κεν δὴ νηῦς πλείη βιότοιο γένηται,
ἀγγελίη μοι ἔπειτα θοῶς ἐς δώμαθ’ ἱκέσθω·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote ken dē nēus pleiē biotoio genētai,
angeliē moi epeita thoōs es dōmath’ hikesthō·
sentences.l:
but when indeed the ship full of livelihood has become,
news to me then swiftly to the house let come;
sentences.i: But once the ship is full of supplies, let news come to me quickly at the house;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ὅτε κεν δή ... γένηται 'but when once it has become': ὅτε κεν with the subjunctive. νηῦς is the Ionic form of ναῦς 'ship'; πλείη is the epic feminine of πλεῖος 'full' (a relative of πλήρης), with βιότοιο 'of livelihood, of supplies', a genitive. ἀγγελίη 'news'; ἱκέσθω is the aorist imperative of ἱκνέομαι 'come', 'let it come'; ἐς δώμαθ’ is εἰς δώματα 'to the house'; θοῶς 'swiftly' is the adverb of θοός.

sentences.t: οἴσω γὰρ καὶ χρυσόν, ὅτις χ’ ὑποχείριος ἔλθῃ·
sentences.tr: oisō gar kai chryson, hotis ch’ hypocheirios elthēi·
sentences.l: for I will bring gold too, whatever under-hand may come;
sentences.i: for I will bring gold as well, whatever comes within my reach;
sentences.n: She promises gold. οἴσω is the future of φέρω 'I will bring'. ὅτις χ’ is ὅτις κε, 'whatever'; ὑποχείριος 'under the hand', that is within reach; ἔλθῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ἔρχομαι 'come'.

sentences.t: καὶ δέ κεν ἄλλ’ ἐπίβαθρον ἐγὼν ἐθέλουσά γε δοίην.
sentences.tr: kai de ken all’ epibathron egōn ethelousa ge doiēn.
sentences.l: and indeed something else, a boarding-fare, I, willing at least, would give.
sentences.i: and I would gladly give something else besides, as my fare.
sentences.n: καὶ δέ κεν 'and indeed ... would'; ἄλλ’ is ἄλλο 'something else'. ἐπίβαθρον 'fare, passage-money' is a rare word taken from ἐπιβαίνω 'step on board'. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ; ἐθέλουσά γε 'willing, at least' is a feminine participle (the speaker is a woman); δοίην is the optative of δίδωμι, 'I would give'.

sentences.t:
παῖδα γὰρ ἀνδρὸς ἑῆος ἐνὶ μεγάροις ἀτιτάλλω,
κερδαλέον δὴ τοῖον, ἅμα τροχόωντα θύραζε·
sentences.tr:
paida gar andros heēos eni megarois atitallō,
kerdaleon dē toion, hama trochoōnta thyraze·
sentences.l:
for a child of a good man in the halls I am nursing,
gainful, indeed, of such a kind, together running outside;
sentences.i: for I am bringing up in the halls the child of a good man, a shrewd child indeed, who runs out of doors beside me;
sentences.n: She names what she will add to the price: a child of the house. παῖδα γὰρ ἀνδρὸς ἑῆος: ἑῆος is the epic genitive of ἐΰς 'good', 'of a good man', the man of the house; the child is not named. ἐνὶ μεγάροις 'in the halls'; ἀτιτάλλω 'I nurse, bring up'. κερδαλέος 'gainful, shrewd' comes from κέρδος 'gain'; δὴ τοῖον 'of just such a kind'. ἅμα τροχόωντα θύραζε 'running along out of doors': τροχόωντα is the uncontracted accusative participle of τροχάω 'run', and θύραζε has the suffix -ζε, like -δε, 'to the door, outside'.

sentences.t:
τόν κεν ἄγοιμ’ ἐπὶ νηός, ὁ δ’ ὑμῖν μυρίον ὦνον
ἄλφοι, ὅπῃ περάσητε κατ’ ἀλλοθρόους ἀνθρώπους.
sentences.tr:
ton ken agoim’ epi nēos, ho d’ hymin myrion ōnon
alphoi, hopēi perasēte kat’ allothroous anthrōpous.
sentences.l:
him I would bring to the ship, and he would earn for you a numberless price
wherever you sell him among men of other speech.’
sentences.i: I would bring him to the ship, and he would fetch you a price beyond counting, wherever you sell him among men of another tongue.’
sentences.n: She makes the child the bait for the sailors. τόν κεν ἄγοιμ’ 'him I would bring': κεν with the optative ἄγοιμι 'I would lead'; ἐπὶ νηός 'to the ship', νηός being the genitive of ναῦς. ὁ δ’ 'and he'; μυρίον ὦνον 'a numberless price'; ἄλφοι is the aorist optative of ἀλφάνω 'earn, bring in'. ὅπῃ περάσητε 'wherever you sell (him)': the aorist subjunctive of περάω. κατ’ ἀλλοθρόους ἀνθρώπους 'among men of other speech' (ἀλλόθροος joins ἄλλος 'other' to θρόος 'speech').
